African sacred ibis (Threskiornis aethiopicus) chicks emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days], a developmental period that is broadly consistent with that of other medium-sized threskiornithids. The incubation temperature, maintained through constant brooding by both parents, is critical for proper embryonic development. Upon hatching, these altricial nestlings are relatively small, with a wet weight at birth measured at 39.5 grams [Wwb = 39.5 grams]. This neonatal mass represents a modest investment per offspring, yet the species compensates through high parental provisioning rates and a relatively short nestling period. The rapid growth trajectory of the chicks is supported by a diet of insects, small aquatic invertebrates, and occasional vertebrate prey, all gathered from shallow wetlands and mudflats. Parental care is intensive, with both adults sharing brooding and feeding duties over the first few weeks post-hatching, a common strategy among colonially nesting waterbirds.

Under the sustained body temperatures characteristic of active foraging adults in this species, approximately 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones is observed. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and first departure from the nest, occurs at 37.5 days after hatching [tx = 37.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This relatively rapid transition to flight capability allows young ibises to escape nest predators and begin exploring foraging habitats alongside their parents. Sexual maturity, or puberty, is attained considerably later, at 112.5 days after hatching [tp = 112.5 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the substantial investment in somatic growth required before the onset of reproductive physiology at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. The interval between fledging and puberty is characterized by a prolonged juvenile phase during which young birds refine their foraging skills, establish dominance hierarchies within feeding flocks, and gradually acquire the plumage characteristics of adults. Field observations indicate that this post-fledging period is energetically demanding, with juvenile mortality rates remaining elevated until individuals achieve full independence and foraging proficiency.

The onset of first reproduction in African sacred ibis is not immediate upon reaching sexual maturity, as individuals typically defer breeding while they acquire nesting territories and establish pair bonds. The time since birth at first brood has been recorded at 1,095 days [tR = 1,095 days] under the thermal conditions typical of their active metabolic range (40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]). This three-year delay between reaching puberty and initiating a first clutch is a common life-history pattern among long-lived colonially nesting waterbirds, reflecting the time required to secure a suitable nest site within dense breeding colonies, often amidst other ciconiiform species. First-time breeders generally produce smaller clutches than experienced adults, and reproductive success increases with age and site fidelity. The extended pre-breeding period also allows young ibises to accumulate sufficient endogenous reserves to sustain the high energetic costs of egg production, incubation, and chick provisioning, which are particularly demanding given the species' reliance on ephemeral wetland food resources.

Maximum recorded longevity for the African sacred ibis under field conditions is estimated at 13,505 days [am = 13,505 days], or approximately 37 years, in individuals maintained at 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This impressive lifespan places the species among the longer-lived members of the Threskiornithidae family, a trait linked to its relatively low extrinsic mortality rate as a large-bodied, socially dominant bird with few natural predators. Reproductive output is correspondingly modest; females typically produce up to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = up to 2 eggs per clutch], with a single brood raised annually [F_R_i = single brood raised annually]. The combination of small clutch size, extended parental care, and deferred maturity underscores a slow life-history strategy geared toward high adult survival rather than high fecundity. Body mass shows pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a common pattern among ibises where males invest heavily in territorial defense. Adult females attain an ultimate wet weight of 1,424.5 grams [Wwi = 1,424.5 grams], while males are substantially larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 1,572.75 grams [Wwi = 1,572.75 grams].

The thermal physiology of the African sacred ibis is tightly linked to its life-history timing, as the standard active metabolic temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C] provides a stable internal environment for critical developmental and reproductive processes. This elevated body temperature, typical of endothermic birds, supports the rapid growth rates observed in nestlings and the high metabolic demands of flight and foraging. The species exhibits pronounced ecological flexibility, breeding across a wide range of African wetlands from the Nile Delta to southern Africa, and has successfully colonized urban and agricultural landscapes where it forages in landfills, pastures, and irrigation canals. This dietary and habitat plasticity has contributed to population expansions in several regions, though local declines linked to wetland drainage and pesticide use have been documented. Interestingly, the incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] is slightly lower than the adult active body temperature, a difference that reflects the thermal requirements of embryonic development and the insulating properties of the nest structure. Ongoing climate change may alter the availability of suitable breeding habitats, potentially disrupting the synchrony between peak food availability and the species' tightly scheduled reproductive cycle.
